question: Why can't you use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with credentials: true?

options.text: Wildcard origin doesn't work in Chrome
options.explanation: Allow-Origin: * works in all browsers, but only without credentials. With credentials: true, a specific origin is required -- this is a CORS specification requirement, not a browser-specific issue

options.text: Cookies aren't sent with wildcard due to a bug in the fetch API
options.explanation: This isn't a bug but an intentional security restriction. If wildcard worked with cookies, any site could send requests with the user's cookies to your API
Wildcard origin works fine with HTTPS. The restriction is security-related: with credentials: true, the server must explicitly specify a trusted origin to prevent CSRF

options.text: The CORS specification forbids wildcard with credentials -- the browser requires a specific origin for cookie security

question: Why send the X-RateLimit-Reset (Unix timestamp) header in rate limiting responses?

options.text: Without this header, the CDN won't cache the response
options.explanation: CDN caching depends on Cache-Control, not X-RateLimit-Reset. Rate limit headers inform the client about limits, not for caching purposes

options.text: It's an HTTP standard -- without it, the request will be rejected
options.explanation: X-RateLimit-* headers are not an HTTP standard -- they're a convention. Requests won't be rejected without them, but the client won't be able to intelligently plan retries

options.text: The client can calculate when to send the next request and implement exponential backoff or wait
The browser automatically retries the request after Reset
options.explanation: The browser doesn't process X-RateLimit-Reset automatically. This is information for client-side code to implement retry logic with proper timing

question: How does the Token Bucket algorithm differ from Fixed Window for rate limiting?

options.text: Fixed Window is more accurate, while Token Bucket is approximate
options.explanation: Fixed Window is actually less accurate due to the boundary burst issue (2x burst). Token Bucket provides smoother rate limiting while supporting legitimate burst patterns

options.text: Token Bucket allows burst traffic (a series of requests in a row), gradually replenishing tokens, while Fixed Window counts within a rigid window
Token Bucket is faster because it doesn't store request history
options.explanation: Fixed Window also doesn't store history -- only a counter. The difference is in behavior: Token Bucket allows bursts up to maxTokens, then limits to refillRate

options.text: Token Bucket only works with Redis, while Fixed Window works in memory
options.explanation: Both algorithms can be implemented in memory or with Redis. The difference is in the model: Token Bucket uses tokens + refill, Fixed Window uses counter + reset

question: When should a server return 304 Not Modified?

options.text: Automatically for all GET requests after the first one
options.explanation: 304 is not automatic -- the client must send conditional headers (If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since). Without them, the server returns a full 200 response
Idempotency is not related to 304. The server returns 304 only when the client sends an ETag (If-None-Match) or date (If-Modified-Since) and the data hasn't changed

options.text: When the client sent If-None-Match with an ETag matching the current one -- data hasn't changed, no need to send the body
When the client repeats the same request within max-age
options.explanation: Within max-age, the browser uses the cache and doesn't make a request to the server at all. 304 is returned for conditional requests with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since
